newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: WTO delegates fly home, shop after final party.
newsitem.headline: WTO delegates fly home, shop after final party.

text.p: Trade ministers from 128 nations and a supporting cast of officials began returning home on Saturday after a final colourful party to wind up the weeklong World Trade Organisation (WTO) ministerial meeting.

Fireworks lit the night sky on Friday after a one-hour long song-and-dance programme for the WTO delegates featuring artists such as Britain's Sarah Brightman and former Tony award winner Lea Salonga of the Philippines.
Lion dancers pranced and huge drums thundered on Sentosa, a small resort island dubbed the Disneyland of Singapore.

The ministers finished lengthy negotiations on Friday to put the world on track towards free trade in the 21st century with a string of ground-breaking agreements they claim would unshackle global business and help the poor.
The U.S. delegation, headed by Acting Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky, did not stay for the celebrations, flying out of this city-state immediately after the conference ended.
"We'll celebrate on the plane," a member of the U.S. delegation told the Straits Times newspaper in remarks published on Saturday.
Barshefsky headed to Tokyo for last-ditch talks to resolve a dispute over deregulation of the Japanese insurance market before a Sunday deadline.
Some delegates said they would stay for at least a day to take in some sightseeing and do a little bit of shopping. Others said they planned to just sleep in their hotel rooms.
"I'm going to sleep until noon. I haven't had any this week," one Asian diplomat said.

The ministers hailed a hard-earned pact to scrap tariffs on information technology by the end of the century as a triumph that showed the fledgling trade body is now a powerful new actor on the world economic stage.
The agreement on an Information Technology Agreement (ITA) will eliminate barriers in the rapidly growing $600 billion world market in computer-related products.
"The ministerial conference has been an outstanding event in all respects," Singapore's trade minister and conference chairman Yeo Cheow Tong said to applause from fellow ministers.

"I regard it as astonishing that we've been able to bring together such a diverse group of countries and get agreement on a text that is not just papering over the cracks but genuinely important," European Union Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan said.
WTO Director-General Renato Ruggiero claimed the outcome will affect the poorest "man in the street".
Economists said the ITA would boost the information technology industry, especially in Asia, and eventually lead to lower prices for a vast range of consumer goods that use electronic parts.

Barshefsky said 28 countries, representing 84 percent of global trade in information technology products, had already signed the agreement and another six were committed to signing, thus bringing total coverage to more than 90 percent.

A hard-fought compromise on the link between trade and the divisive issue of labour standards enabled the United States and its European allies on one side and developing nations such as India, Indonesia and Malaysia on the other to proclaim victory.
